title: Deleting One Gene in a Whole Mouse

scenes.tts: Cell culture cannot show blood pressure or nervous-system wiring. Before gene targeting, a mouse geneticist could add DNA at random, but could not choose which gene to change. So how do you test what one gene does in a whole animal?
scenes.visual: A dish of cells with crossed-out chips (blood pressure, wiring) beside a mouse; DNA bits land at random on a chromosome bar while a target reticle is crossed out; then one gene chip with a question mark and an arrow to the mouse.
scenes.narration: Cell culture cannot show blood pressure or nervous-system wiring. Before gene targeting, a mouse geneticist could add DNA at random, but could not choose which gene to change. So how do you test what one gene does in a whole animal?

scenes.tts: Embryonic stem cells, or E S cells, come from the early embryo and can still contribute to any tissue. A targeting vector carries DNA matching the gene on both sides of the change: two homology arms. Between them sits a neomycin resistance marker. Outside them sits a thymidine kinase marker. Electroporation puts the vector in. In rare cells, homologous recombination swaps the vector's version into the gene's own place.
scenes.visual: Embryo gives ES cells in a dish; zoom into one nucleus with the gene on a chromosome bar; the vector with arms, neo and tk lines up above it; a bolt carries it in; arms cross over and the gene block is replaced by the vector's version.
scenes.caption: Embryonic stem cells, or ES cells, come from the early embryo and can still contribute to any tissue. Electroporation puts the vector in. In rare cells, homologous recombination swaps the vector's version into the gene's own place.

scenes.tts: A drug, G four eighteen, kills cells with no vector. A correct swap loses the thymidine kinase gene, which lies outside the matching DNA. A random insertion keeps it, and thymidine kinase makes ganciclovir toxic. Survivors are screened by P C R or Southern blot, then expanded.
scenes.visual: Three cells with mini genomes: no vector, random insertion (neo and tk), correct swap (neo only). G418 kills the first; ganciclovir kills the second; the third survives, is screened, and grows into a clone.
scenes.caption: A drug, G418, kills cells with no vector. A correct swap loses the thymidine kinase gene, which lies outside the matching DNA. A random insertion keeps it, and thymidine kinase makes ganciclovir toxic. Survivors are screened by PCR or Southern blot, then expanded.

scenes.tts: E S cells are injected into blastocysts of a strain with a different coat colour, and foster mothers carry the embryos. The pups are chimeras, part host and part E S cell, and coat colour shows the share. A chimera, usually male, is typically mated with a black strain. Agouti pups come from E S derived germ cells, and tail D N A shows if they carry the allele. These are usually heterozygous. Further breeding gives homozygotes.
scenes.visual: Brown ES cells are injected into a black-outlined host blastocyst, carried by a foster mother; a chimera with brown patches on black; mated with a black mouse; litter of agouti and black pups, tail DNA test on an agouti one; heterozygous pair breed to a homozygous mutant.

scenes.tts: At the cell stage, Koller and Smithies found two correct colonies among two hundred thirty-four resistant ones. In mice, the phenotype is read by comparing homozygous null with wild-type. Track A null mice lose sympathetic neurons and many sensory neurons. Their superior cervical ganglion forms normally, then loses its neurons from embryonic day fifteen point five. Survival, not birth, failed.
scenes.visual: A grid of 234 colonies with two highlighted; then a wild-type and a null ganglion drawn side by side and an idealised neuron-number timeline that tracks together until embryonic day 15.5, then the null falls.
scenes.caption: At the cell stage, Koller and Smithies found two correct colonies among 234 resistant ones. In mice, the phenotype is read by comparing homozygous null with wild-type. scenes.tts: First, genetic background. The targeted gene is flanked by E S cell DNA, which may carry its own mutations. Caspase three null mice on one strain died perinatally with exencephaly. On another strain they reached adulthood with minimal brain pathology. So backcross to a defined strain, and compare wild-type animals of the same background. Second, compensation. Myo D null mice had normal muscle and raised myf five. So delete related genes together.
scenes.visual: Left: one knockout allele on two strain backgrounds with different outcomes, flanking ES DNA marked, control: backcross and compare. Right: knock out gene A, its relative B rises and covers; control: delete both.
scenes.caption: First, genetic background. The targeted gene is flanked by ES-cell DNA, which may carry its own mutations. Caspase-3-null mice on one strain died perinatally with exencephaly. On another strain they reached adulthood with minimal brain pathology. So backcross to a defined strain, and compare wild-type animals of the same background. Second, compensation. MyoD-null mice had normal muscle and raised Myf-5. So delete related genes together.

scenes.tts: Bax null mice, studied in 1995 and 1998 by Knudson and White with colleagues, had naturally occurring neuron death largely eliminated. A deletion in every cell could do that. In 2004, Glebova and Ginty combined Bax null with N G F null, so N G F's role in target innervation could be tested without neurons dying.
scenes.visual: A nerve with a few axons in wild-type, more axons in Bax-null, then a second knockout (NGF) added: the neurons stay and target innervation can be read. Tags: Knudson 1995; White 1998; Glebova and Ginty 2004.
scenes.caption: Bax-null mice, studied in 1995 and 1998 by Knudson and White with colleagues, had naturally occurring neuron death largely eliminated. A deletion in every cell could do that. In 2004, Glebova and Ginty combined Bax-null with NGF-null, so NGF's role in target innervation could be tested without neurons dying.

scenes.tts: In 1997, Howell and colleagues deleted Dab1, and the brain copied the reeler brain. Reeler itself is a spontaneous mutant, not a knockout. In 1999, Trommsdorff and colleagues removed both ApoER2 and VLDLR, and the phenotype mimicked reeler. Knock-ins change a gene instead of deleting it. In 2004, Fagiolini and colleagues put in a diazepam-insensitive alpha one or alpha two subunit. They found that alpha one circuits drive the critical period. A knockout shows necessity, not sufficiency.
scenes.visual: Reeler mutant brain beside Dab1 knockout and ApoER2/VLDLR double knockout looking alike; then a knock-in swaps one subunit in a receptor; then the rule. Tags: Howell 1997; Trommsdorff 1999; Fagiolini 2004.
